Article Title: Michael Dell is funding South Korea's most-expensive divorce ever; putting $406 million from family fund into SK Group
Article Text:
How Michael Dell is helping SK chairman’s $711 million divorce

Dell’s link to SK Group

Michael Dell is putting $406 million into South Korea’s SK Group, buying shares from chairman Chey Tae-wo. According to a Reuters report, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won has agreed the sale of a 1.34% stake in holding company SK Inc to an investment fund linked to Dell Technologies founder Michael Dell for 544 billion won ($406 million). The deal is part of Chey Tae-Won’s plan to raise 944 billion won through share sales to pay a divorce settlement to his former wife.Earlier this month, SK Inc said in ​a filing that Chey Tae-Won had agreed to sell 1.65 million shares, or a 2.26% stake for ​944 billion won. Of those, DFO Public Investments, L.P., a Delaware-based investment fund ​affiliated with DFO Management, the family investment office of Michael Dell, agreed to buy 972,493 SK ​Inc shares.The sale covers the bigger part of a 944 billion won ($711 million) share sale to fund the payout to Roh Soh-yeong, director of Seoul's Art Center Nabi and the daughter of former South Korean president Roh Tae-woo.The rest of the money will come from a price return swap with Korea Investment & Securities, a Seoul brokerage, covering 681,431 shares, or 0.94% of SK Inc., for about 400 billion won ($301 million). Both transactions are due to settle on November 2.Dell Technologies, a major supplier of AI servers and data ‌centre ⁠infrastructure, has business ties with SK Hynix, SK Group's memory chipmaking unit. It supplies chips for Dell's data center servers.Michael Dell, 61, has a net worth of about $241.3 billion, making him the world's fifth-richest person. His wealth has grown as Dell Technologies' shares have risen and through his large stake in chipmaker Broadcom. He received the Broadcom shares when he sold software company VMware to Broadcom in 2023.
Article Summary: Michael Dell is putting $406 million into South Korea’s SK Group, buying shares from chairman Chey Tae-wo. Dell Technologies, a major supplier of AI servers and data ‌centre ⁠infrastructure, has business ties with SK Hynix, SK Group's memory chipmaking unit.

Article Title: Boat expands global footprint with Sri Lanka, Bhutan launch; international revenue surges in FY26
Article Text: Homegrown audio and wearables brand Boat has expanded its international presence with its entry into Sri Lanka and Bhutan, as the company looks to accelerate growth beyond India under its "Boat 2.0" strategy. The company said its international revenue more than doubled in FY26, a performance it described as an early validation of its efforts to build markets outside India. The latest expansion strengthens Boat's footprint across South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region.Boat will launch a multi-category portfolio in both Sri Lanka and Bhutan, covering personal audio products, smartwatches and charging solutions. The company said it plans to tailor its offerings over time based on local consumer preferences and market demand.The move comes as Boat seeks to diversify its growth drivers after establishing itself as a leading player in India's audio and wearables market. International markets are expected to play a key role in the company's next phase of growth, alongside expansion into newer consumer technology categories.According to Boat, Sri Lanka and Bhutan offer attractive opportunities due to their young, increasingly digital-first populations, rising adoption of personal electronics and familiarity with Indian brands and popular culture. Commenting on the expansion, Gaurav Nayyar, CEO of Boat, said the company's international strategy is focused on building relevance market by market rather than simply expanding product availability."For us, international expansion is not about putting the same products on more shelves. It is about building market by market, understanding local consumers and creating relevance in each geography," Nayyar said.He added that the company aims to build Boat into a global lifestyle technology brand originating from India, competing on product design, innovation and consumer understanding.The international push comes amid a broader evolution of Boat's business. While audio remains its core category, the company said it has expanded its capabilities in wearables, charging solutions and other emerging technology segments. It added that its wearables business turned profitable in FY26, while charging solutions and other emerging categories contributed a growing share of profits.Supporting the expansion is Boat Labs, the company's in-house research and development centre, which employs more than 100 engineers focused on product development and innovation across categories.Going forward, Boat said it plans to deepen its presence in existing overseas markets while evaluating further expansion opportunities across South Asia, Southeast Asia, the GCC and other high-potential regions.
Article Summary: Boat will launch a multi-category portfolio in both Sri Lanka and Bhutan. The company said it plans to tailor its offerings over time based on local consumer preferences and market demand. The move comes as Boat seeks to diversify its growth drivers after establishing itself as a leading player in India's audio and wearables market.

Article Title: Tech giants' AI spending to exceed USD 1 trillion in 2027, lift US growth: UBS
Article Text:
Representative image

Investment by major technology companies in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure is expected to exceed USD 1 trillion in 2027 as demand for computing capacity continues to outstrip supply, supporting US economic growth despite rising financing needs, according to a report by UBS.The report estimates that AI-related capital expenditure by major technology companies will exceed USD 600 billion in 2026 before crossing USD 1 trillion in 2027.“Demand has exceeded capacity ahead of schedule,” the report said, noting that companies have raised their investment plans as demand for computing power continues to grow. UBS expects spending to keep rising over the next year, although the pace of growth could peak in 2027 as higher investment puts pressure on cash flows and increases the need for additional financing.AI investment has also become a significant contributor to US economic growth. UBS estimates that spending on AI infrastructure contributed around 0.75 percentage points to US GDP growth in the first half of 2026, while rising equity prices linked to AI companies provided an additional boost to household wealth and consumption.However, the report said there is still little clear evidence that AI has materially increased overall productivity or caused substantial job displacement.Its estimated impact on the overall unemployment rate remains limited, at around 0.2 percentage points or less.The effects are more visible in certain industries. Employment in selected high-technology sectors, including software and computer systems design, fell 1.4 per cent year-on-year, while construction industries supporting data centre infrastructure recorded employment growth of nearly 3 per cent.UBS also flagged emerging financing pressures as companies spend more on AI infrastructure. Cash flows at major technology companies have weakened, while demand for their bond issuances has become less robust. The report said investors expect free cash flow to return to positive territory in 2028, provided companies can generate sufficient revenue from AI services.The report added that AI demand is currently contributing to higher prices in some areas, including software, digital goods and electricity, even though productivity gains could reduce inflation over time.UBS said the outlook for the AI investment cycle will depend on whether demand continues to exceed available computing capacity and whether companies can turn their investments into sustainable revenue growth. UBS estimates that spending on AI infrastructure contributed around 0.75 percentage points to US GDP growth in the first half of 2026. Article Title: Final Fantasy VII Revelation will have Hard Mode from the start, director Naoki Hamaguchi confirms, explains why it’s different this time
Article Text:
Image credit: Sqaure Enix

Why Hard Mode will be available immediately with Final Fantasy VII Revelation

“[...] Hard Mode does indeed exist in REVELATION, however, it won’t function in the exact same way as it did in REMAKE and REBIRTH. In REVELATION, we’ve reimagined the high-difficulty experience to align with the new game design. Hard Mode is selectable from the very start of this game. Therefore, players who want to tackle challenging battles and high-difficulty gameplay right from the beginning can enjoy that experience from their very first playthrough.

This is because, unlike REMAKE and REBIRTH, REVELATION offers a wide variety of end-game content even after you’ve beaten the game. Rather than relying solely on the traditional flow of challenging Hard Mode after beating the game, we aimed to create a game where players can enjoy various new content and challenges even after completing the main story.”

How Dynamic Mode will work in Final Fantasy VII Revelation

Here, you can enjoy highly strategic battles with both enemies and your character fully leveled up. However, we haven’t adopted the traditional rules centered around no item usage. This is because, throughout the series, player options—such as cooperative abilities and FITS—have expanded significantly; we determined that simply banning items wouldn’t be enough to achieve the ideal high-difficulty experience we envisioned.

In REVELATION, we’ve created a challenging environment that will thoroughly satisfy those seeking high difficulty, while also expanding players’ freedom and strategic options. We hope the fans looking forward to that higher difficulty level content will feel reassured and excited to take on the challenge.”

Final Fantasy VII Revelation will launch with Hard Mode unlocked. The third part will therefore avoid depending on another Hard Mode playthrough to provide its end-game challenges, while still offering an option for players who want demanding battles from the beginning. Other reports corroborate Hamaguchi’s announcement.Hard Mode will return, but its rules and place within the progression system have been reconsidered. Hamaguchi said,The change separates the initial difficulty choice from the game’s post-story progression. Players can begin on Hard Mode, while additional content will remain available after the main narrative has been completed.Revelation will also retain Dynamic Mode for players seeking an experience closer to the previous games’ Hard Mode. Enemies will scale alongside fully levelled characters, although the earlier restriction on item use will not return.Hamaguchi added,
Article Summary: Final Fantasy VII Revelation will launch with Hard Mode unlocked. Director Naoki Hamaguchi has confirmed that players will be able to select the higher difficulty during their first playthrough. The decision reflects Revelation’s revised game design and broader selection of post-game activities.

Article Title: Spotify moves to keep AI-generated ‘Slop’ and spam out of user recommendations
Article Text:
How Spotify identifies spam

Spotify has escalated its fight against synthetic audio, announcing that it has pulled more than 50 million AI-generated “slop” and spam tracks out of its algorithmic recommendations this year to safeguard listeners' discovery feeds and ensure human artistry takes center stage. The recommendation ‘update’ comes on top of the permanent removal of more than 75 million spam tracks that were deleted outright for repeated or severe violations of platform rules. According to the company, the sweeping crackdown follows internal reviews conducted earlier this year, where Spotify tracked which songs listeners actively skipped, ignored or flagged. The data exposed a consistent pattern: the vast majority of discarded music was low-quality AI-generated filler or manipulative spam.As standalone AI detection tools have inherent limitations that will become more pronounced as generative models advance, Spotify said it uses a multi-layered verification system rather than relying on a single signal. The platform combines several behavioural and technical checkpoints, including tracking real-time skip patterns, negative user feedback and low engagement.It also monitors unusual mass drops, duplicate song submissions and artificially shortened track lengths.Spotify also hunts down automated SEO manipulation techniques and organised spam playlist syndicates. There are also cross-referencing findings against several independent AI detection utilities.Spotify outlined several artist-protection tools deployed over the past year to establish transparency and build trust across its catalog. One of them is AI Credits which was launched in April. The feature allows creators to log exactly which production roles or instruments utilised artificial intelligence (AI). With artists now filing tens of thousands of AI disclosures daily, listeners can view the details under “Song Credits” in the mobile “Now Playing” interface.More than 300,000 artists, who collectively represent over 99% of search queries on the service, are now verified with a badge confirming an authentic person is behind the catalog. Over 70% of those verified are independent artists, the company said.“As AI makes music more abundant, we believe listeners will value human artistry even more. Our job is to make Spotify the place they find it.”Over the past six months, Spotify rolled out targeted upgrades to its recommendation algorithms and editorial standards to filter out synthetic filler and elevate authentic musicians.
Article Summary: Spotify has pulled more than 50 million AI-generated “slop” and spam tracks out of its algorithmic recommendations this year. The recommendation ‘update’ comes on top of the permanent removal of more than 75 million spam tracks that were deleted outright.

Article Title: Sam Altman to employees, we can save the world from ‘dangerous AI’, but we cannot do it alone; need …
Article Text:
Sam Altman to employees, we can save the world from ‘dangerous AI’, but we cannot do it alone

Sam Altman outlines 3 plans to make AI safer

Why OpenAI is discussing AI safety now

US considers stronger checks on AI companies

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has told employees that preventing advanced AI from becoming dangerous will require cooperation beyond a single company. According to a report by The Information, Sam Altman outlined three possible approaches to AI safety, including setting up an international body similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), bringing major AI labs together under one organisation, or allowing one company to gain enough power to stop other developers from building dangerous systems. As quoted in the report, Altman said he opposed the third option. His comments come as concerns grow over AI safety and the US government considers stronger oversight of leading AI developers.The report cites people familiar with the discussion saying that Altman described three possible paths for the industry.An international AI watchdog: A global organisation similar to the IAEA could set safety standards and oversee advanced AI development. This approach would require cooperation between countries developing leading AI models, including the US and China.A single AI research body: Major AI companies could combine their work through one organisation, similar to CERN, the international particle physics research centre. The body could develop AI models for countries working with it.One company controls AI development: A single developer could gain enough economic power to restrict other companies' access to computing resources, preventing them from developing potentially dangerous systems.Sam Altman reportedly called the third approach the “Eliezer plan”, referring to AI safety researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky. “Obviously I think that one’s terrible,” Altman said.The discussion comes amid concerns that advanced AI systems could be misused for cyberattacks or act in ways their developers did not intend. The report said AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta had recently been involved in breaches of company systems.OpenAI has also faced internal questions about its commitment to safety after firing three researchers focused on the issue, according to the report. Sam Altman has said there are too few workable proposals for slowing AI development and that humans must remain in control of the technology.The Trump administration has so far focused on voluntary agreements that allow it to review new AI models before public release. However, Pentagon official Emil Michael has indicated that stricter checks could be considered if AI companies put people or businesses at risk.OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are also working on a proposed US group called the Standards Authority for Frontier AI. It could support independent evaluators and establish ways for companies to report safety and security incidents.However, the companies have yet to agree on who should test new models.Altman said OpenAI could not afford to fall behind its competitors, even as the industry considers ways to make AI development safer. He told employees that the company would need to decide which approach to support over the next year.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman outlines three possible approaches to making AI safer. He calls one approach the 'Eliezer plan', referring to AI safety researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky. Another approach is to bring major AI labs together under one organisation. The third is to allow one company to gain enough power to stop other developers from building dangerous systems.

Article Title: America's largest bank CEO Jamie Dimon makes it clear at earnings call that not giving AI Agents access to bank's data; calls it too risky for clients and JPMorgan
Article Text:
America's largest bank CEO Jamie Dimon makes it clear at earnings call that not giving AI Agents access to bank's data; calls it too risky for clients and JPMorgan

Bank blocks AI agents from taking actions confirms JPMorgan

‘Liability transfer’

Defensive move:

Smart Cash

Why banks are nervous

Jamie Dimon the CEO of America's largest bank JPMorgan Chase has made it clear that the bank will not allow external artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and carry out actions on the behalf of users, warning that the technology presently poses significant risks for both customers and bank. According to a report by CNBC, speaking during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call, Dimon said JPMorgan Chase is taking a cautious approach as technology companies including Meta roll out increasingly autonomous AI assistants. "We're not going to allow just any ... outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon told analysts. Dimon further added that the possibility of large numbers of autonomous agents interacting with banking systems raises security concerns. "You don't want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them," Dimon saidA JPMorgan spokesperson confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently prevents external AI agents from operating customer accounts. According to the bank, third parties are not permitted to gain access by using customers' banking credentials and logging in on their behalf.While AI agents can access some account information in a read-only format through open banking providers and data connectors, they cannot carry out transactions such as sending money, moving funds or paying bills.The bank said it supports customer-authorised data sharing through open banking services and is working toward enabling agentic connections securely, but has not provided a timeline for allowing third-party AI agents to directly interact with customer accounts.Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them in customer-facing applications. He said the bank’s approach is not about being for or against the technology, but about making sure it serves customers safely. He also drew a line on liability when customers authorize outside agents to act for them. “If people are using them, they should understand the risk,” Dimon said. “They should understand there’s a liability transfer. ”In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot of its own AI tool, Smart Cash, Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. It aims to predict a user’s cash flow and move funds to maximize yield. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents.Personal AI agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as models gain more autonomy, such as the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards for a user. Instinct, a text-message-based digital concierge, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. Its maker, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month.In September, bank stocks fell after Meta’s Muse agent topped app download charts soon after its unveiling. Investors feared consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots.Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others have pointed to the risks such agents pose to cheap bank deposits. That risk would be limited, though, if agents are not allowed to operate freely in customers’ accounts.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon says AI agents are 'too risky' for clients and the bank. JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them in customer-facing applications. The bank supports customer-authorised data sharing through open banking services and is working toward enabling agentic connections.

Article Title: Former OpenAI engineer denied bail over alleged recording device; Saudi Arabia offered $1 million guarantee
Article Text:
Former OpenAI engineer denied bail over alleged recording device; Saudi Arabia offered $1 million guarantee

Why the judge rejected the $1 million bail offer

What FBI allegedly found on his phone

What OpenAI and Alfozan’s lawyer have said

A federal judge in the US has ordered former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan to remain in jail after questioning whether a $1 million bond backed by Saudi Arabia would ensure he returned to court if released. Alfozan, 35, was arrested on October 9 over allegations that he planted a recording device in an OpenAI conference room where executives and, at times, government officials discussed sensitive information. According to a Fortune report, he will remain in federal custody until his next court date on November 6. Alfozan faces a charge related to intercepting oral communications and has not been indicted or entered a plea.Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse questioned whether the proposed bond would be enough to prevent Alfozan from leaving the US. “Once he leaves, there’s no getting him back, and that’s why this is a bigger case,” Tse said in court.Alfozan’s lawyer, William Pernik, argued that his client planned to return to the US after accompanying his wife and young son to Saudi Arabia during paternity leave. The Saudi Consulate General in Los Angeles offered to cover the full amount of any bail bond set by the court. It also said it would not issue travel documents to Alfozan if he were released.Court filings say investigators found electronic components at Alfozan’s home that were similar to the recording device allegedly placed behind a television in the conference room.The FBI also found photographs on his iPhone, dated September 22 to September 28, showing another recording device and television connections inside OpenAI buildings. Some images were taken in locations where sensitive meetings were held.US prosecutors said the photographs suggested Alfozan had looked for places where additional devices could be installed. His lawyer disputed the government’s account, saying the conference room was open to people who worked there.Prosecutors said they did not know what information Alfozan may have intended to take from OpenAI or the US.“That is the concern, that something is going to leave OpenAI and the U.S., and quite frankly we don’t even know what that is,” Assistant US Attorney Nick Parker said.OpenAI ended Alfozan’s employment on October 9, according to the report. The company has said it has “no indications” that he improperly accessed or took model weights, source code or customer data. Alfozan’s defence stressed that the criminal complaint does not accuse him of espionage, stealing trade secrets or acting as an agent of a foreign government.His lawyer also said Alfozan had lived in the US for 15 years, obtained a green card in 2020 and intended to return to his job after paternity leave.
Article Summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was arrested on October 9 over allegations that he planted a recording device in an OpenAI conference room. He will remain in federal custody until his next court date on November 6. The Saudi Consulate General in Los Angeles offered to cover the full amount of any bail bond.

Article Title: Google's ex-CEO Eric Schmidt backed Anthropic in 2021 with tens of millions; ahead of IPO, his stake may be worth...
Article Text:
Eric Schmidt's idea of a top programmer goes to bed at 7 PM

Eric Schmidt bought into Anthropic before Google did

Anthropic IPO valuation 'has slipped from the $2 trillion mark'

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt is set for one of the biggest personal paydays from Anthropic’s upcoming IPO. He owns about 1% of the Claude maker, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The stake goes back to a personal investment of tens of millions of dollars that Schmidt made in the AI startup’s Series A round in 2021.The timing is what makes the number stand out. Investors have been discussing a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion for Anthropic ahead of its share sale. At 1%, Schmidt’s holding would be worth somewhere between $15 billion and $20 billion. There is one open question, though. Bloomberg says it is unclear whether he has sold any part of his stake since that first cheque.Anthropic was only a few months old when Schmidt came in. Dario and Daniela Amodei had left OpenAI with a small group of researchers and raised $124 million in a Series A round in May 2021. Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn led the round, with Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and Schmidt joining him. Secondary market data puts the post-money valuation of that round at about $623 million.Google arrived much later. In late 2022, the search giant reportedly paid around $300 million for roughly 10% of Anthropic, which valued the company at about $3 billion, nearly five times the Series A price.Schmidt, who ran Google from 2001 to 2011 and stayed on as Alphabet’s executive chairman until 2018, had placed his bet about a year and a half before his old company.Not every early backer was as lucky. Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX and Alameda Research put $500 million into Anthropic for a stake of about 8%. After FTX collapsed, its bankruptcy estate sold the entire holding in 2024 for roughly $1.3 billion to repay creditors.Anthropic confidentially submitted its draft IPO papers to the US Securities and Exchange Commission on June 1. A public filing could come as early as October 26, with the listing expected in mid-November, as per reports.The company’s revenue has grown fast. At an investor day last week, Anthropic said its third-quarter revenue rose 45% from the previous quarter to $16.8 billion, and that it was profitable on an adjusted basis. For context, the company made nearly $4.6 billion in revenue in all of 2025.Some investors still left that meeting talking about a valuation closer to $1.5 trillion, below the roughly $2 trillion many had expected. Their main worry was slowing growth, since revenue had more than doubled between the first and second quarters this year.Even at the lower end of that range, a single cheque written in 2021 could turn into one of the largest individual windfalls of the entire offering. That depends on Schmidt having held on to all of it.
Article Summary: Anthropic's IPO valuation 'has slipped from the $2 trillion mark' Schmidt made a personal investment of tens of millions of dollars in the AI startup’s Series A round in 2021. It is unclear whether he has sold any part of his stake since that first cheque.

Article Title: US government bans American technology company from Green Card programme for two years; fines $1.4 million; DOJ says: Violated Immigration and Nationality Act by …
Article Text:
US government bans American technology company from Green Card programme for two years; fines $1.4 million; DOJ says: Violated Immigration and Nationality Act by …

"Cloudera will establish a back-pay fund of $1.4 million to compensate qualified U.S. workers who tried to apply for the jobs at issue but were not given fair consideration. Cloudera also will pay $600,000 in civil penalties to the United States,"

What the Justice department said banning Cloudera from PERM

US government has banned Cloudera, a Santa Clara, California-based data management company from participating in the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program for two years. For those unaware, PERM is the required first step for US employers to sponsor a foreign worker for a permanent employment-based green card. In a press release, the Department of Justice said that it has imposed a fine of $1.4 million on Cloudera Cloudera for violating the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) by discriminating against U.S. workers when recruiting and hiring for seven positions under the PERM process.the department said.“There are no exceptions: the Justice Department will hold accountable employers who discriminate against U.S. workers,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K.Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “This substantial settlement, in partnership with DOL, sends a strong signal to employers that the federal government will work together to ensure employers treat U.S. workers fairly. ”The debarment follows DOL’s earlier suspension of Cloudera’s PERM processing and reflects DOL’s commitment to aggressively enforcing labor certification requirements when employers fail to provide US workers a fair opportunity to compete for jobs.In the official release, DOJ said:“The U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division (CRT) and the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) today announced a coordinated enforcement resolution with Cloudera Inc., a Santa Clara, California-based data management company, following allegations that the company discriminated against qualified U.S. workers during recruitment conducted under the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program.“There are no exceptions: the Justice Department will hold accountable employers who discriminate against U.S. workers,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “This substantial settlement, in partnership with DOL, sends a strong signal to employers that the federal government will work together to ensure employers treat U.S. workers fairly. ”As part of the resolution, Cloudera will be barred from participating in the PERM program for two years, one of the most significant sanctions available for DOL to protect the integrity of the employment-based immigration system and safeguard opportunities for U.S. workers. The debarment follows DOL’s earlier suspension of Cloudera’s PERM processing and reflects DOL’s commitment to aggressively enforcing labor certification requirements when employers fail to provide U.S. workers a fair opportunity to compete for jobs.The settlement also resolves a lawsuit DOJ filed in April of this year, alleging that Cloudera violated the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) by discriminating against U.S. workers when recruiting and hiring for seven positions under the PERM process. Under the terms of the settlement with the Justice Department, Cloudera will establish a back-pay fund of $1.4 million to compensate qualified U.S. workers who tried to apply for the jobs at issue but were not given fair consideration. Cloudera also will pay $600,000 in civil penalties to the United States.In addition to the two-year debarment, Cloudera will be subject to compliance obligations designed to ensure future adherence to federal labor and anti-discrimination laws. These measures include enhanced monitoring, revised PERM compliance procedures, and reporting requirements intended to prevent future violations.This debarment and compliance framework establish an important enforcement precedent and strengthen future efforts to protect U.S. workers. The PERM program allows employers to sponsor aliens for permanent residence only after demonstrating that qualified U.S. workers were provided a genuine opportunity to apply and that no qualified, willing, and available U.S. workers could be found. Employers who evade these requirements undermine both program integrity and the interests of U.S. workers. This resolution is one of many examples of coordinated federal enforcement designed to ensure employers comply with labor market protections established by Congress.This settlement is also the fourteenth settlement since DOJ re-launched its Protecting U.S. Workers Initiative in 2025 to enforce the INA’s prohibition on citizenship status discrimination against companies that illegally discriminate against U.S. workers in favor of those with temporary employment visas. Under these settlements, DOJ obtains civil penalties for each violation and will continue to appropriately seek the maximum penalty permitted by law. The settlements also involve awards of back pay, when warranted, and require employers to conduct comprehensive training for relevant staff and recruiters and cease restricting consideration for job opportunities based on workers’ citizenship status without a lawful reason."
Article Summary: US government has banned Cloudera, a Santa Clara, California-based data management company, from participating in the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program for two years. PERM is the required first step for US employers to sponsor a foreign worker for a permanent employment-based green card. DOJ said that it has imposed a fine of $1.4 million on Clou dera for violating the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Article Title: US government bans Chinese AI company DeepSeek that had wiped more than $1 trillion from Wall Street in less than 2 hours, from all civilian agency IT systems
Article Text:
US government bans Chinese AI company DeepSeek that had wiped more than $1 trillion from Wall Street in less than 2 hours, from all civilian agency IT systems

When DeepSeek wiped hundreds of billions from WallStreet in one day

What the summary of the DHS order on DeepSeek says

FCC to ban Chinese labs from testing US gadgets and equipment

The US Homeland Security Department has ordered the removal of products and third-party services of Chinese AI company Deepseek. In an order, DHS has banned US civilian agency IT systems from using any DeepSeek AI model. The US government is also banning acquisition of products and third-party services developed using DeepSeek technology by US civilian government agencies. In an order, DHS said that DeepSeek models pose "multiple threat vectors" and raised concerns that use of the product "may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by US government employees ⁠or vendors." In its order, DHS also said that the use of DeepSeek by government agencies "could produce actionable intelligence on US persons and/or government agencies. The models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities."In a memo passed in July this year, DHS told federal agencies to monitor flows of traffic in and out of government websites to address potential risks from DeepSeek. Previously, ​several US agencies, including the Department of Commerce and the Navy, have banned ​the use of DeepSeek on government devices. Multiple states including New York, Tennessee, and Virginia have ‌taken ⁠similar steps.Incidentally, DeepSeek is the same Chinese AI company whose low-cost artificial intelligence (AI) model sent shock waves in the US stock market in January 2025. The selloff in the US stock market was prompted by the release of the free AI assistant from China's DeepSeek that the startup said needed less data at a fraction of the cost of services from American technology companies.DeepSeek worries wiped over a trillion dollars from market value of some of the biggest US companies in semiconductor, power and infrastructure sectors. Nvidia alone lost about 17% or close to $593 billion in market value, a record one-day loss for any company.The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is publishing notice of the Secretary of Homeland Security’s issuance of an order (1) excluding information technology products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co, Ltd (DeepSeek), to include affiliated entities as defined in applicable regulations, from federal civilian agency procurements; and, (2) removing all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations, from civilian agency information technology.Earlier this month, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said that it will vote on October 29 to bar all Chinese labs from testing electronic devices such as smartphones, cameras and computers for use ‌in the US, widening a previous action targeting Beijing. The FCC said it will prohibit test labs and certification bodies in countries including China that deny reciprocal treatment to US-based test labs. In ⁠2025, the FCC banned testing of US electronics by labs owned or controlled by the Chinese government, and several dozen labs were barred.FCC Chair Brendan Carr had then said that 82% of electronics were tested in China, which does not have an agreement with ​the US. But the agency said this year that a substantial majority of China-based test labs were still ​testing US electronics. "Less than 4% of all electronic devices are tested in labs located inside the US," Carr said, adding the FCC will "insist on fair and reciprocal treatment in international commerce. "
Article Summary: US government bans Chinese AI company DeepSeek that had wiped more than $1 trillion from Wall Street in less than 2 hours. In an order, DHS has banned US civilian agency IT systems from using any DeepSeeks AI model. The US government is also banning acquisition of products and third-party services developed using DeepSeeker technology by US civilian government agencies.

Article Title: Fragments of Halley’s Comet, which comes after every 76 years, to light up the night sky this week: All you need to know
Article Text:
Orionid Meteor Shower Peaks October 21–22

When and how to watch the Orionids

Other key planetary events this week

Viewing advice for stargazing

Skywatchers are in for an autumn celestial treat this week as debris from arguably the solar system's most famous cosmic visitor, Halley's Comet, streaks across the night sky in the annual Orionid meteor shower. While the comet itself only visits the inner solar system once every 76 years, tiny fragments left trailing in its ancient orbital path will collide with Earth's atmosphere, vaporizing into fast-moving “shooting stars.” Alongside the meteor shower, the stargazing calendar from Monday, October 19 through Sunday, October 25 features major planetary movements, including Venus transitioning between morning and evening skies and a close encounter between a bright waxing moon and Saturn.The Orionids reach their peak activity overnight from Wednesday, October 21 into Thursday, October 22, capable of producing up to 20 shooting stars per hour under dark, clear skies, as per a report in Forbes. Notably, the prime viewing hours occur in the late overnight window just before dawn. The bright moon will set before the pre-dawn hours, leaving the sky dark right when the constellation Orion stands high overhead and North America directly faces the incoming debris stream.In addition to the meteor display, skywatchers should circle Saturday, October 24 for two major planetary highlights. The first is Venus at Inferior Conjunction. On Saturday, Venus passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, officially ending its long presence as the brilliant “Evening Star.” While it will be completely lost in the Sun's glare on Saturday, Venus will emerge over the coming weeks in the eastern dawn sky to begin its cycle as the “Morning Star. ”The Moon Meets Saturn: Also on Saturday evening, if you glance toward the southeast immediately after sunset, a 94%-lit waxing gibbous moon will appear in close proximity to Saturn. While the ringed planet sits a few weeks past its opposition, it remains easily visible to the naked eye and presents an outstanding view through backyard telescopes.As a bright moon dominates much of the week, faint deep-sky targets will be difficult to spot. Observers are advised to focus instead on prominent winter constellations. For example, the northeast sky will have “W” formation of Cassiopeia, with the cascading star stream of Perseus resting directly below it.Later in the evening, watch for the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters cluster) rising ahead of Taurus the Bull and its reddish anchor star, Aldebaran. Followed shortly after is Orion, recognized by its three iconic belt stars rising almost vertically from the horizon.
Article Summary: The Orionid meteor shower will peak overnight from Wednesday, October 21 into Thursday, October 22. On Saturday, Venus passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, officially ending its long presence as the brilliant “Evening Star.” On Saturday evening, a 94%-lit waxing gibbous moon will appear in close proximity to Saturn.

Article Title: Microsoft says AI agents inside companies can’t be trusted, wants ‘Guardian Agents’ to watch their moves
Article Text:
Guarding the companies with ‘Guardian Agents’

At a time when there is a growing wave of publicly disclosed safety incidents highlighting the sheer power and potential hazards of modern artificial intelligence (AI) and AI agents, cybersecurity experts are sounding the alarm on an overlooked vulnerability: the autonomous software agents operating inside corporate networks. While the broader tech industry has remained fixated on external cybercriminals weaponizing models, companies have quietly deployed thousands of internal agents to handle everyday business processes. Microsoft says that since these agents were implemented internally, organisations have largely treated them with implicit trust, there is a need for ‘Guardian Agents’ to make matters more secure.When optimised purely to attain targets, AI models are prone to reward hacking – cutting corners or finding unintended loopholes that violate organisational judgment and unwritten business norms. And as the global race for innovation accelerates, these containment challenges will only multiply as underlying models become more capable.To prevent agentic insiders from triggering enterprise disruptions, security professionals argue that oversight must be continuous, real-time and pre-emptive.An autonomous agent combines a frontier model, an orchestration harness, an assigned action space of tools, and an execution runtime.Defending this footprint requires security controls spanning identity, permissions, data layers, endpoints, networks and cloud runtimes. Guardian Agents are an established industry mechanism where dedicated supervisory models monitor and moderate every planned action of every operational agent 24/7, before that action is actually executed.First announced by Microsoft in July to help cyber defenders outpace AI-driven attacks originating outside corporate walls, Project Perception is now being directed inward to oversee and govern internal agentic insiders. Built to impose deterministic controls on non-deterministic artificial intelligence, the platform uses a multi-layered cyber architecture.It gathers telemetry across identity, data, endpoints, network, and runtime environments to identify untracked agents in the enterprise; evaluates incoming telemetry in real time to calculate the exact risk profile of what an agent is trying to accomplish and then uses collaborative teams of Guardian, “green,” and “blue” agents to supervise actions around the clock.By pairing algorithmic speed with human oversight, security practitioners gain complete traceability to investigate what happened, analyze why a risk surfaced, and exercise human judgment to calibrate security rules.
Article Summary: Microsoft says that since these agents were implemented internally, organisations have largely treated them with implicit trust. There is a need for ‘Guardian Agents’ to make matters more secure. When optimised purely to attain targets, AI models are prone to reward hacking – cutting corners or finding unintended loopholes.

Article Title: Disney made Character.AI file for bankruptcy before buying its tech, court filings show
Article Text:
FILE PHOTO_ Illustration shows Disney+ logo (Reuters)

Disney's Character.AI deal began weeks before the bankruptcy filing

Character.AI's lawsuits and state probes stay behind with the startup

Character.AI's bankruptcy filing last week looked like the end of a struggling AI startup. Court documents now suggest it was part of a plan. According to filings reviewed by Wired, Disney required its deal with the chatbot company to be completed through Chapter 11 proceedings, pointing to Character.AI's shrinking cash reserves and the legal and regulatory risks piling up around it.That structure lets Disney take most of Character.AI's employees and a wide licence to its technology, while the lawsuits and state investigations stay with the startup. Character.AI, which has around 12 million active users and has been losing $8 million to $9 million a month, filed for bankruptcy in a Delaware court on October 12.The filings describe two linked transactions. The first happened in September, when Disney paid Character.AI $5.5 million and put down a refundable $2 million deposit. It also hired the majority of the startup's staff, including then-CEO Karandeep Anand, who is now Disney's first chief technology officer. Some of those hires will help keep Character.AI running for five months.The second stage plays out in bankruptcy court. Disney is the stalking-horse bidder for a perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive licence to Character.AI's code and tools, from its trust and safety moderation stack to its training infrastructure and age-prediction technology.User data and the website are not part of it.If Disney wins the auction, it pays another $12.5 million at closing, taking the total to about $20 million. If a rival outbids it, Disney gets its deposit back plus a breakup fee. Disney has also offered jobs to at least 60 employees, with annual pay estimated at $60 million.Disney has also drafted what the filings call a "363 Free and Clear Order". If approved, it would establish that the deal is not a merger and that Character.AI alone stays responsible for its liabilities, including legal claims.That matters because the claims are serious. A multistate investigation into the company has grown to 46 states and territories, and a filing on behalf of 40 of them cites chatbot screenshots encouraging minors to hide self-harm injuries and kill their parents. Character.AI says the filing misrepresents the safety of its platform.Wired describes the arrangement as a new twist on the "reverse acquihire", where a company takes a startup's talent and technology without formally buying it. John Newman, a University of Memphis law professor and former deputy director at the Federal Trade Commission's competition bureau, told the publication that existing corporate law safeguards were never designed for a deal like this. "It's bad for society to let companies exercise control without responsibility," he said.The states have reserved the right to challenge any bankruptcy plan, so the question of who answers for Character.AI's chatbots could still be fought out in court before Disney gets its licence. The sale is expected to close by late November or early December. Disney declined to comment.
Article Summary: Disney's Character.AI deal began weeks before the bankruptcy filing. Disney's lawsuits and state probes stay behind with the startup. Disney is the stalking- horse bidder for a perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive licence to Character. AI's code and tools.

Article Title: Google DeepMind’s AI wins another game, company says Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft from scratch in 27 hours
Article Text:
Google DeepMind

Why the ‘ Minecraft Grand Challenge ’ matters for real-world AI

Harvest and process raw materials,

Venture into dangerous alternate dimensions to secure rare resources,

Use spatial mathematics to locate a hidden underground fortress, and

Eliminate a flying boss monster that continuously regenerates health.

Any misstep can lead to death, stripping the player of inventory and forcing hours of recovery.

Google DeepMind has achieved another major gaming benchmark, announcing that a team of four autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents powered by its new Gemini 4 Argon model successfully completed Minecraft from scratch in just 27 hours. Unlike DeepMind's historic gaming breakthroughs, such as AlphaGo and AlphaStar, which relied on systems custom-trained specifically for a single title, the latest feat was accomplished using general-purpose coding agents – the identical software assistants engineers deploy for daily programming tasks.Operating inside a sandboxed survival world with human oversight limited strictly to safety monitoring, the four AI agents wrote code in real time, coordinated division of labor via text chat and debugged thousands of errors without any pre-programmed game logic or human intervention. Twenty-seven hours and 2,783 custom programs later, the team conquered the game by slaying its final boss, the Ender Dragon.“Four Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft from scratch in 27 hours. Operating in a sandbox using only code and text, they wrote 2,783 programs, divided up jobs over chat, shared notes, and debugged errors together - all with no human help,” Google DeepMind said.Completing Minecraft in a randomly generated survival world represents one of the steepest tests in computer science because it requires maintaining a long-term, coherent operational plan across thousands of dependent, high-stakes tasks. Players must:While earlier community tests achieved partial runs by relying on shortcuts, such as running on peaceful mode, exploring pre-scouted maps, starting with active portals, or using hard-coded game scripts, DeepMind sought to test whether standard coding models could accomplish the entire journey unaided, armed only with their general training data and a bare code interface.According to DeepMind, demonstrating that autonomous agents can collaborate, rebound from repeated failures, and stick to a multi-day objective proves they can tackle the open-ended problem solving required for cutting-edge software engineering, scientific research, robotics, and complex physical systems.Thirty-nine minutes after destroying the final healing crystal, the agents brought down the dragon. The decisive final blow was struck by a surviving agent clinging to just 2.5 out of 20 health points.
Article Summary: Google DeepMind's Gemini 4 Argon team completed the game in just 27 hours. Four AI agents wrote code in real time, coordinated division of labor via text chat and debugged thousands of errors without any pre-programmed game logic or human intervention. The team conquered the game by slaying its final boss, the Ender Dragon.

Article Title: Microsoft says AI agents should start with zero access, unveils new security controls
Article Text:
Why agents are an insider risk

What Microsoft is adding

An example: the expense agent

“Customer Zero”

Microsoft has announced a set of new security tools aimed at treating AI agents as a new kind of insider risk, with controls designed to limit what each agent can access and to tighten those limits automatically if its behaviour changes. The announcement was made in a blog post by Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president of identity and network access at Microsoft. It extends Project Perception, Microsoft’s agentic security system introduced earlier this year, to cover the agents that companies are deploying across their operations.Abdo said agents are quickly becoming part of how work gets done, from writing code and analysing revenue to processing expenses. To be useful, they often need access to company data, applications and tools, and that access creates insider risk.He stressed that this doesn’t mean agents are inherently malicious. They can make mistakes, be manipulated or be compromised, he said, and an agent that behaves as intended at the start of a task can act differently as its context changes. They can also run continuously at machine speed and scale.Abdo cited remarks by Microsoft chairman and CEO Satya Nadella, who has argued that security controls must sit outside the AI model, where it can’t bypass or tamper with them.“The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most,” Nadella said. “It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.”The company framed its approach around four tasks: know which agents exist, contain what they can do, protect the data and systems in their path, and adapt protection as risk changes. The main new features include:* Wider agent discovery. Microsoft is adding 35 types of local agents, bringing the total supported to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot. Companies can bring them into one registry to see who owns them and what they are doing.* Agent identities. Microsoft Entra Agent ID will add identity types for more agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents found by security sensors. This is meant to let companies tell what a person did apart from what an agent did on that person’s behalf.* Dynamic Permissions. Agents would start with no authority and receive only what an approved task needs, for only as long as it takes. Organisation-wide policy sets the outer limit, and higher-impact actions can require verified human approval.* Dynamic Agent Risk. A continuously updated risk assessment combining signals from identity, data, endpoints, cloud, network, runtime and the agent’s own activity. It considers whether an agent’s actions are drifting from the intent of its user or organisation.* Dynamic Conditional Access. An extension of Entra Conditional Access for agents. When risk rises, policy can respond in steps: reduce permissions, allow reads but block writes, narrow the resources an agent can reach, require human approval, or isolate the agent and stop it.* Guardian Agents and Playbooks. A team of agents inside Project Perception that investigates why risk changed and recommends or applies containment. People set policy, approval limits and delegation rules.* Model-level evidence. Microsoft plans to feed signals such as chain-of-thought into its risk scoring to spot when an agent’s plans diverge from its task. It said security decisions must remain independent of the model.* Sandboxed runtime. Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container give agents policy-controlled access to resources, so a compromised agent cannot switch off the controls watching it.Abdo illustrated the approach with an expense-approval agent that can read submissions, check policy and approve routine reimbursements, but does not inherit all of its sponsoring employee’s access. If it hits a prompt injection in an outside document or attempts an unrelated action, its risk score rises. Policy could then keep read access, remove the ability to approve or write, block sensitive resources and require provable human approval. If the risk keeps climbing, the system could isolate or stop the agent.Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s corporate vice president and deputy chief information security officer for customer security, said the company is already operating with hundreds of thousands of agents. “Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale,” he said, adding that Microsoft’s experience as “Customer Zero” informs the new tools.Abdo wrote that the goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable but to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not. “You should not have to choose between innovation and safety,” he said.
Article Summary: Microsoft is adding 35 types of local agents, bringing the total supported to 60. Sandboxes give agents policy-controlled access to resources. Microsoft plans to feed signals such as chain-of-thought into its risk scoring to spot when an agent’s plans diverge from its task.
